name: OTP solicited from the recipient under a pretext
description: The sender asks the recipient to disclose an OTP, supported by a pretext, pressure or an identity claim. The discriminating feature is direction: a message DELIVERING an OTP is legitimate infrastructure and must never match. Suppression carries that distinction.

source_references.document_ref: Reserve Bank sensitises members of public on safe use of digital transactions (2020-06-22)
source_references.quote: banks and other payment systems operators never ask for details such as password, PIN, OTP, CVV number

lifecycle.$comment_separation_of_duties: Early review_due set deliberately: SRC-004 is from 2020 and is the oldest source underpinning any published rule (G-14).

explanation.plain: Someone has asked you to share a one-time password. No bank, payment company or government body will ever ask you for an OTP — the Reserve Bank of India says so directly. Sharing it lets them act on your account.
explanation.technical: CREDENTIAL_REQUEST_OTP matched together with a pretext, identity claim or pressure indicator, spanning at least two evidence classes. Four suppressors guard the legitimate-delivery case; the rule cannot fire on a message that merely contains the word OTP.
verification_steps: Read the message again: is it giving you a code, or asking for one? Only the second is a scam.
Call your bank on the number printed on your card, not any number in the message.
explanation.why_confidence_limited: Confidence is reduced when the pretext is generic and no institution is named, since ordinary users do sometimes relay codes to family.

provenance.notes: The research package specified this as a keyword trigger on 'OTP, one-time password, share code, verification code', which fires on a bank's own anti-fraud SMS (CONF-002, seed case B-001). Encoded here as a combination with explicit suppression instead.
